analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and manufacture of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 179 House members including the Democratic leader, never left the Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, or transfer semiautomatic assault weapons and ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. People who already legally owned these guns could keep them, but any future sale or transfer would have to go through a licensed gun dealer with a background check. The bill also requires secure storage of grandfathered weapons, new serial-number markings, and lets local governments use federal grant money to fund gun buy-backs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by mass shootings and everyday gun violence, since the weapons and magazines most often used in high-casualty shootings could no longer be newly manufactured or sold to civilians. Law enforcement keeps its exemptions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of communities affected by gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons — a category covering AR-15 and AK-type rifles, certain pistols and shotguns, and bump-stock-type rate-of-fire devices — and magazines holding more than 10 rounds.

Grandfathers weapons lawfully owned before enactment: owners could keep them, but private sales or transfers would have to go through a licensed dealer with a background check, and grandfathered assault weapons must be securely stored where a prohibited person could reach them.
Requires serial numbers and manufacture dates on new assault weapons and magazines, and requires police to be notified when a prohibited person tries to buy a grandfathered assault weapon.
Allows state and local governments to use existing federal justice-assistance grant funds to pay people who turn in assault weapons or large magazines through buy-back programs.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and dealers lose the ability to make and sell the banned models going forward, and gun owners who want to buy these weapons or large magazines in the future can no longer do so. Existing owners keep their guns but face storage and transfer rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and future buyers

drawbacks.text: The definitions are broad: a semiautomatic rifle becomes banned if it has a detachable magazine plus any single feature such as a pistol grip, threaded barrel, or barrel shroud, and common handguns with outside-the-grip magazines are covered, so the ban reaches many ordinary firearms beyond military-style rifles.

Existing weapons stay legal and transferable (with background checks), so the ban does not remove the millions of grandfathered assault weapons already in circulation — it only stops new ones from being made and sold.

Supporters of gun rights argue the ban restricts commonly owned firearms protected by the Second Amendment and that criminalizing possession by otherwise law-abiding owners burdens people rather than criminals; that objection was never tested in a floor debate here.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill would trade a real restriction on what guns civilians can newly buy for a potential reduction in high-casualty shootings; it spares current owners by grandfathering their weapons. The main honest objections are its feature-based breadth — which sweeps in ordinary hunting and self-defense firearms — and the fact that grandfathering means the existing stock remains legal for decades. Whether the safety benefit justifies the burden on manufacturers and buyers is the core disagreement, and this Congress never debated it on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the Assault Weapons Ban of 2018 on February 26, 2018, with 178 cosponsors.
All 178 cosponsors were Democrats, and the list included House Democratic Leader Nancy Pelosi and Majority Whip Steny Hoyer, giving the bill the full weight of House Democratic leadership.
The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and on March 20, 2018, referred it to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the bill's last action was the subcommittee referral, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers kept selling semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines with no new federal restrictions, and no member of the House ever had to record a vote on the ban.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Assault Weapons Ban of 2018 on February 26, 2018.

for.name: 178 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Democratic Leader and Majority Whip.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: The Judiciary Committee, which received the bill on the day it was introduced, took no action on it — no hearing or markup — before sending it to a subcommittee where it stalled.

against.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote, which it could not have reached without his scheduling decision.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed bans on semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines and pressured lawmakers against them during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — all 178 cosponsors were Democrats, none of the chamber's 235 Republicans sponsored or cosponsored — and Republicans controlled the committee and floor calendar that the bill never got past.

industries.note: The bill makes it a crime to manufacture or sell the listed semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines over 10 rounds, cutting off future sales of the industry's most popular modern rifle platforms. Manufacturers would keep profiting from grandfathered transfers, but the new-gun market closes.

Dealers could no longer sell banned weapons or large magazines going forward, which shrinks their product lines, but the bill routes all grandfathered private sales through licensed dealers with background checks, giving dealers a paid role in every future transfer.

industries.industry: Gun owners who want to buy these firearms
industries.note: Current owners keep their guns, but future purchases of the covered rifles, pistols, shotguns, and 10-plus-round magazines would be illegal. The cost falls on buyers and on manufacturers, not on people who already own the guns.
